hook_text: Bloemfontein, 8 January 1912. A young lawyer told a hall full of leaders: we are one people.
clip_script: In 1910, four colonies became the Union of South Africa. Only white men could sit in its Parliament. African leaders had petitioned, written and travelled to London. Nothing changed. So a lawyer named Pixley ka Isaka Seme sent out a call: bury the old divisions, Xhosa and Zulu, Sotho and Tswana. We are one people. On 8 January 1912, chiefs, teachers, ministers, lawyers and journalists met in Bloemfontein. They formed the South African Native National Congress. John Dube was president. Sol Plaatje was secretary-general. Their tools were petitions, newspapers and delegations. Within a year they faced the Land Act. In 1923 the Congress took a new name: the African National Congress.
visual_style: A whiteboard map with separate regional circles joining into one large circle at Bloemfontein, with name cards for Seme, Dube and Plaatje and a timeline to 1923.
pacing: Steady build to the founding, then a quick look ahead.
